title: Rafael and the Debt
premise: Tamsin Amberdale, a former financial-crimes analyst turned whistle-blower, has spent six years buried under four identities after testifying against the Verrone family's laundering network. When a burner phone arrives containing recordings only her dead handler could have made, she is lured into extracting Marek Verrone—the patriarch's estranged son, who claims he can collapse the empire from inside. But Marek is bait in a trap set by the very prosecutor Tamsin once trusted, who sold out to the family years ago. To survive, Tamsin must weaponize the debt the Verrones owe her: the ledger she hid before disappearing. In the end, she trades the ledger for Marek's life, burns her fourth and final name, and walks into the open—visible at last, but free.
about_author: Lior Marchetti is the pen name of a former compliance officer who spent a decade inside the machinery of international finance before leaving it behind for fiction. They write thrillers about ordinary people trapped in systems built to outlast them.

chapters.title: Four Names
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A quiet morning in a rented flat in Porto is interrupted by routine tradecraft: checking for tails, rotating cash, rehearsing her cover story as 'Nadia.' The chapter establishes her discipline and loneliness. Emotional beat: controlled paranoia masking exhaustion.

chapters.title: The Package That Wasn't Ordered
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A courier delivers a padded envelope containing a burner phone and a photograph of Tamsin's real face—a face no living person should possess. The phone rings once. She doesn't answer. Beat: dread crystallizing into certainty that her cover is blown.

chapters.title: A Voice Six Years Dead
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She finally answers; the voice belongs to Daniel Reyes, her handler, who officially died in 2019. He gives her thirty seconds of proof—a detail only he knew—and one instruction: be at the Alfama funicular at midnight. Beat: grief and fury colliding.

chapters.title: Funicular
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: brief interlude from Marek Verrone, held in a safehouse, counting tiles. Back to Tamsin at the meeting point, where instead of Daniel she finds a dead drop and a dossier on Marek. Beat: the trap's shape becomes visible.

chapters.title: The Son Who Walked Out
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Flashback to his defection: stealing his father's books, contacting an EU prosecutor named Ilse Brandt, and realizing too late that Brandt's protection was a leash. Present day: his guards change, and he understands he's being moved—or disposed of. Beat: cornered intelligence.

chapters.title: Brandt
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She investigates Ilse Brandt, the prosecutor who once promised her immunity, and finds offshore traces of Verrone money flowing toward a foundation Brandt chairs. The betrayal reframes everything: Daniel's death may have been Brandt's doing. Beat: cold rage replacing fear.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Owes
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She retrieves the hidden ledger—the full Verrone account trail she secreted before vanishing—from a storage unit in Bilbao. Opening it means becoming visible again. She decides the debt cuts both ways now. Beat: resolve hardening into intent.

chapters.title: Extraction Terms
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The phone rings again; 'Daniel' offers terms: extract Marek from a transfer convoy outside Seville, and Daniel returns her original testimony file—the one thing keeping the Verrones hunting her. She negotiates brutally. Beat: agency reclaimed through bargaining.

chapters.title: Convoy Math
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Inside the moving convoy, Marek maps his captors' routines, noting one guard who never checks his phone and one who checks it too often. He leaves a message scratched into the door panel: coordinates. Beat: patience as resistance.

chapters.title: Seville, 4 A.M.
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The extraction: a staged breakdown, a stolen ambulance, ninety seconds of chaos on the A-49. It works—but the too-attentive guard escapes with his phone intact. Beat: adrenaline followed immediately by the sick drop of a loose end.

chapters.title: Two Liars in a Room
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Tamsin and Marek, holed up in a farmhouse, interrogate each other. He reveals Brandt planned to trade him back to his father; she reveals the ledger exists. Neither fully believes the other. Beat: wary alliance forged from mutual usefulness.

chapters.title: The Guard Who Checked Twice
chapters.summary: Antagonist POV (the escaped guard, reporting to Brandt). We learn Brandt orchestrated everything—including 'Daniel's' voice, which is AI-reconstructed from old case calls—to force Tamsin to surface and retrieve the ledger for her. Beat: dramatic irony tightening the noose.

chapters.title: Dead Man Dialing
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She runs voice analysis on the burner calls and confirms the reconstruction. Whoever holds Daniel's archive also holds proof of how he died. Grief becomes evidence. Beat: mourning converted into method.

chapters.title: The Father's Offer
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Old man Verrone reaches Marek directly: come home, disown the ledger, and live. Marek records the call. His father's tenderness is more frightening than his threats. Beat: filial love revealed as the deepest corruption.

chapters.title: Household of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Safehouse compromised; they relocate through Andalusian backroads while Tamsin pieces together Brandt's endgame: a public prosecution of the Verrones using sanitized evidence, with the real ledger destroyed and Marek silenced after testifying. Beat: the clock audibly ticking.

chapters.title: Ambush at the Salt Flats
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Brandt's team corners them near Santa Pola. Marek is taken; Tamsin escapes with the ledger and a bullet graze, forced to choose between fleeing clean or walking into custody to save him. Beat: sacrifice made explicit.

chapters.title: Turning Herself In
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She contacts a journalist with the ledger as insurance, then surrenders to Brandt under negotiated terms: Marek lives, she hands over the ledger. Brandt agrees too easily. Beat: apparent defeat concealing a gambit.

chapters.title: The Room Where It Happens
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Held in the same safehouse where the story began, Marek stalls his father's men and passes Tamsin's hidden message—copied ledger fragments already sent to three newsrooms—through a sympathetic guard. Beat: hope smuggled through cracks.

chapters.title: Ledger Day
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Handover meeting. Tamsin reveals the ledger she surrendered is partial—and authenticated fragments are publishing within the hour unless Brandt releases them both and confesses to Daniel's murder on record. Beat: climax; power inverted through exposure.

chapters.title: Collateral
chapters.summary: Climax continues, dual POV. Verrone's men, learning of the publications, move to erase everyone—father and prosecutor alike become liabilities. In the chaos, Marek frees himself; Brandt is arrested by her own colleagues as the story breaks worldwide. Beat: institutions devouring their own.

chapters.title: Settlement
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Aftermath: the elder Verrone indicted, Marek entering witness protection on his own terms, Daniel posthumously cleared. Tamsin declines new identities. The debt is settled—not forgiven, settled. Beat: weary, earned catharsis.

chapters.title: One Name
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue. Months later, she testifies publicly under her own name, then walks out of the courthouse into an unremarkable street with no go-bag, no burner, no alias. She keeps the dead phone as a reminder. Beat: visibility chosen at last—freedom without safety, embraced anyway.
